Key changes in Wnt and TGFB family pathways associated with regulating regenerative vs

Model of key changes in Wnt and TGFβ family pathways associated with regulating regenerative vs. fibrotic repair Based on the transcriptional analysis there is the potential for distinct regulation of canonical and noncanonical Wnt signaling and TGFβ family pathways associated with regenerative wound healing vs. fibrosis. (A) Key changes associated with canonical and noncanonical Wnt signaling: 1) Engagement of distinct Wnt ligands and FZD receptors to drive differential signaling in response to lens injury. 2) Discrete extracellular environments. During wound healing Wnt signaling may be dampened by an extracellular environment rich with Wnt inhibitors, including sFRPs and CER1. In contrast, fewer families of Wnt inhibitors are upregulated with fibrosis countered by increased expression of extracellular Wnt activators, RSPOs to enhance Wnt signaling, accompanied by increased accumulation of Dishevelled. 3) Intracellular regulation of β-catenin ubiquitination may be upregulated with wound healing vs. fibrosis to also dampen canonical Wnt signaling due to increased expression of genes involved in β-catenin ubiquitination (RBX1, BTRC) (highlighted within the boxed region). Still, there is the potential to control Wnt signaling with fibrosis at the transcriptional level due to upregulation of CBY1 and TLE4 (see box). 4) Lastly, there is the potential to specifically activate the Wnt–Ca2+ pathway via NFAT1 and NFAT2 during fibrosis. (B) Key changes associated with the TGFβ superfamily: 1) Wound healing is accompanied by a potential increase in BMP signaling due to increased SMAD1 expression, as well as by an increase in expression of IDs. 2) Fibrosis is associated with the potential to augment TGFβ signaling due to increased expression of TGFβ signaling components: elevated TGF-β ligand and receptor expression and increased SMAD3 effector and thrombospondin 1 to activate TGFβ. Increased LTBP1 may promote increased storage of latent TGF-β binding to the extracellular matrix (ECM) for later activation. 3) Elevated INHBA and activin receptors may augment activin signaling pathways with fibrosis. 4) The BMP signaling pathway and environment for fibrosis is complex, involving increased expression of pathway elements to promote BMP signaling, including BMP ligands and receptors countered at the same time by an increased expression of extracellular inhibitors FST, CER1, and NOG2 to limit BMP signaling. Increased expression of BMP4 and BMP7, well known antagonists of TGFβ are also present, which may limit the amplitude of the fibrotic response. 5) Lastly, ID function, potentially downstream of TGFβ and/or BMP signaling was found to be required for both regenerative and fibrotic repair.
